Some sectors create lots of jobs but find it hard to get bank credit: small farmers, tiny enterprises, poor households, students. RBI therefore makes banks lend a minimum share of their credit to them. That share is Priority Sector Lending.

A8:
Syllabus: FTP — structural changes in the 1990s · FTP 2015-20 · challenges for the next FTP · FDI, FII and recent trends · Economic development vs growth. 30 PYQs.

1. Foreign Trade Policy

  • Framed by the Ministry of Commerce (DGFT) under the Foreign Trade (Development & Regulation) Act, 1992.
  • 1990s structural change: before 1991 India was protected by high tariffs, licences and quotas. From 1991 came lower tariffs, removal of licensing and quantitative restrictions, a market-based rupee and EXIM policies — a sharp break from protectionism.
  • FTP 2015-20 (extended to March 2023):
    • MEIS — duty-credit scrips of 2–5% of FOB value for goods.
    • SEIS — for services.
    • Both were replaced by RoDTEP (2021), which refunds embedded taxes such as electricity duty and mandi tax, and RoSCTL for garments.
  • FTP 2023 (1 Apr 2023, no end date):
    • Four pillars: Incentive to Remission; Export promotion through Collaboration (states, districts, Indian missions); Ease of Doing Business; Emerging Areas (e-commerce, Districts as Export Hubs, SCOMET).
    • Target: $2 trillion of exports by 2030.
    • Also: an amnesty scheme for EPCG/AA defaults, international trade in INR, and new Towns of Export Excellence.
  • Niryat Bandhu (DGFT): mentoring and outreach for new and potential exporters (no subsidies).
  • Challenges for the next FTP: WTO-compatibility of incentives, protectionism abroad, logistics cost, services exports, FTAs, CBAM and other green barriers.

3. FII / FPI

  • Portfolio investment in shares and bonds: short-term "hot money", hedge funds, volatile, can exit quickly. Registered with SEBI (FPI Regulations 2019).
  • An FPI may hold below 10% of a company's equity. At 10% or more, the holding is treated as FDI.
  • FDI is long-term, builds productive capacity and brings technology and management.
  • VRR (Voluntary Retention Route, RBI 2019): FPIs get relaxed debt-investment norms if they retain the investment for a minimum period.

Developing economy indicators: low per capita income and productivity, high population growth, a large share of labour in agriculture, unemployment, poverty and low human development. A highly diversified, technologically advanced industry marks a developed economy.

A10:
Syllabus: Core elements of sustainable development · Global issues & initiatives · India's progress on SDGs incl. climate change · CSR activities. 30 PYQs — CSR alone was asked in 6 sessions.

1. Sustainable development and SDGs

  • Sustainable development (Brundtland Report, 1987): development that meets present needs without compromising the ability of future generations to meet theirs. Three pillars: economic growth, social inclusion, environmental protection.
  • SDGs ("Transforming our World: the 2030 Agenda"):
    • Adopted by the UN General Assembly in Sept 2015; in force 1 Jan 2016 – 2030.
    • 17 goals, 169 targets. They replaced the 8 MDGs (2000–2015).
    • Built on the 5 Ps: People, Planet, Prosperity, Peace, Partnership.
  • Selected goals: 1 No Poverty · 2 Zero Hunger · 3 Good Health · 4 Quality Education · 5 Gender Equality · 6 Clean Water & Sanitation · 7 Affordable & Clean Energy · 8 Decent Work & Economic Growth · 9 Industry, Innovation & Infrastructure · 11 Sustainable Cities · 13 Climate Action · 14 Life below Water · 15 Life on Land · 17 Partnerships.
  • India: NITI Aayog coordinates and publishes the SDG India Index; MoSPI owns the indicator framework. CSR activities map onto SDGs 1, 2, 3, 4, 6 and others.

2. Climate change — global and India

  • UNFCCC (1992) → Kyoto Protocol (1997) → Paris Agreement (COP-21, 2015): keep warming well below 2°C and pursue 1.5°C, through nationally determined contributions (NDCs).
  • India's Panchamrit (COP-26, Glasgow 2021):
    1. 500 GW of non-fossil capacity by 2030.
    2. 50% of energy requirements from renewables by 2030.
    3. Cut projected emissions by 1 billion tonnes by 2030.
    4. Cut the carbon intensity of the economy by 45% by 2030 (updated NDC: 45% below 2005 levels).
    5. Net zero by 2070.
  • Also from India: International Solar Alliance (2015, HQ Gurugram); OSOWOG (One Sun One World One Grid — a global solar grid, launched at COP-26 with the Green Grids Initiative); Mission LiFE; Plastic Hackathon target of no single-use plastic by 2022; Green Credit Programme and Carbon Credit Trading Scheme (2023).
  • RBI and banks:
    • Sustainable Finance Group in the Department of Regulation (2021), to suggest strategies and regulation for sustainable practices and climate risk.
    • Green Deposit framework (2023): deposits allocated to renewable energy, energy efficiency, clean transport, climate adaptation, pollution control. Fossil fuels, nuclear and large hydro are excluded.
    • Green bonds (most with 5–10 year tenors; also issued by the World Bank for Indian projects); Sovereign Green Bonds (2023).
  • ESG: environmental, social and governance criteria used by responsible investors to screen investments. Good governance serves all stakeholders over the long term, not just short-term shareholders.

B2:
Syllabus: Demand schedule · Forces behind the demand curve · Shifts in demand · Supply schedule & forces · Shifts in supply · Equilibrium · Effect of shifts · Interpreting price & quantity changes.

Demand

  • Demand schedule: a table of the quantity bought at each price. Law of demand: price ↑ → quantity demanded ↓ (other things constant), so the demand curve slopes downward.
  • Why it slopes down: the substitution effect (a dearer good is replaced by cheaper substitutes) and the income effect (a higher price lowers real income). Diminishing marginal utility also contributes.
  • Exceptions:
    • Giffen goods — inferior staples whose demand rises with price (Robert Giffen).
    • Veblen goods — prestige goods, "conspicuous consumption" (Thorstein Veblen).
    • Expectations of further price rises.
  • Forces (determinants): own price, consumers' income, prices of related goods (substitutes and complements), tastes, population, expectations.
  • Movement along the curve = change in the good's own price. Shift of the whole curve = change in any other factor.

Supply

  • Supply schedule and curve: price vs quantity producers are willing to sell. It slopes upward.
  • Shifts come from input costs, technology, prices of other goods, taxes/subsidies, number of sellers, weather.

Equilibrium and shifts

ChangeEquilibrium priceEquilibrium quantity
Demand ↑ (shift right)↑↑
Demand ↓↓↓
Supply ↑ (shift right)↓↑
Supply ↓ (shift left)↑↓

Interpreting data: if price and quantity rise together, demand has shifted. If price falls while quantity rises, supply has shifted.

Equilibrium calculation: Qd = 100 − 4P and Qs = 28 + 2P. Set them equal: 100 − 4P = 28 + 2P → P = 12. Then Q = 100 − 48 = 52.
A fall in the good's own price causes a movement, not a shift. Demand depends on income too. "Substitution effect only" is wrong — both effects work.
B3:
Syllabus: What is money · Money supply · Inflation · Causes of inflation · Measures of inflation.

1. Money

  • Functions: primary — medium of exchange (removes the need for a double coincidence of wants) and measure of value. Secondary — store of value and standard of deferred payment. Money does not itself create production capacity.
  • Kinds: commodity money; fiat money (value by government order — our notes); fiduciary money (based on trust — cheques, drafts); legal tender (must be accepted — notes and coins).
  • Issue: RBI issues all banknotes except the ₹1 note. The Government of India issues the ₹1 note and mints all coins. Notes can legally be issued up to ₹10,000. ₹2000 notes were withdrawn from circulation in May 2023 but remain legal tender.

2. Money supply measures (RBI)

MeasureCompositionName

M1Currency with public + demand deposits with banks + other deposits with RBINarrow money (most liquid)
M2M1 + savings deposits with post office savings banks

M4M3 + all deposits with post office savings organisation (excluding NSCs)Broadest, least liquid
  • Money multiplier = M3 ÷ M0 (Friedman & Schwartz). A higher CRR means a lower multiplier.
  • Velocity of money = Nominal GDP ÷ M3 — how many times a rupee is spent on output in a year.
  • Sources of M3 = net bank credit to government + bank credit to the commercial sector + net foreign exchange assets of the banking sector + government's currency liabilities to the public − net non-monetary liabilities of the banking sector.

3. Inflation — meaning and types

Inflation is a sustained rise in the general price level, meaning the purchasing power of money falls.

By speedRate (indicative)

Walking / trotting3–10%

HyperinflationExtremely high (e.g., 50%+ a month)

Demand-pullAggregate demand rises faster than supply ("too much money chasing too few goods")Big government spending plus tax cuts; credit boom
Cost-pushCosts of key inputs rise where there are no suitable substitutesCrude-oil spike; wage push; monsoon failure in food

  • Headline = all items. Core = headline minus food and fuel (volatile items).
  • Deflation: the price level falls (negative inflation). Disinflation: inflation is positive but falling (6% → 4%). Stagflation: high inflation + stagnant growth + unemployment. Reflation: deliberate policy to lift prices and output after a slump.
  • Who gains from unexpected inflation: borrowers and the Government (debt). Who loses: lenders, depositors, fixed-income earners and pensioners.
  • Real interest rate ≈ nominal rate − inflation (Fisher). An FD at 7% with 5.1% inflation earns about 1.9% real.

  • Fiscal: cut government spending, raise taxes, reduce the deficit.
  • Supply-side: imports, buffer stocks, removing bottlenecks.

  • WPI has no services.
  • Coins are issued by the Government, not RBI.

  • Velocity uses nominal GDP.

Syllabus: Classical theory · Keynes' liquidity preference · Money demand curve · Equilibrium in the money market · Effect of increase in money supply · Shifts in liquidity preference · Hicks-Hansen IS-LM.

TheoryInterest is the price of…Determined byKey names
Classical ("demand and supply theory of capital")Saving / capitalDemand for investment = supply of savings. Interest is the reward for waiting/abstinenceMarshall, Fisher, Pigou
Loanable funds (neo-classical)Loanable fundsDemand and supply of loanable funds (savings + bank credit + dishoarding)Robertson, Ohlin
Liquidity preferenceParting with liquidityDemand for money and supply of moneyJ.M. Keynes (critic of the classical theory)

Keynes: why people hold money

  • Transactions motive: day-to-day spending; depends on income.
  • Precautionary motive: emergencies; also depends on income.
  • Speculative motive: to profit from future bond-price changes; depends inversely on the rate of interest.
  • The money demand (liquidity preference) curve slopes downward against the interest rate. The money supply is fixed by RBI (vertical). Their intersection gives the equilibrium interest rate.
  • Money supply ↑ → interest rate ↓ (until the liquidity trap, where people hold any extra money and the rate cannot fall further).
  • Income ↑ → money demand shifts right → interest rate ↑.

IS-LM (Hicks-Hansen synthesis of Keynesian theory)

  • IS curve: goods-market equilibrium (Investment = Saving). Downward-sloping in (income, interest) space.
  • LM curve: money-market equilibrium (Liquidity preference = Money supply). Derived from Keynes' liquidity preference theory. Upward-sloping.
  • The intersection fixes equilibrium income and interest rate together.
  • Fiscal policy (government spending, taxes) shifts IS; monetary policy (money supply) shifts LM.
There is no "preference motive". The LM curve comes from liquidity preference, NOT the classical theory. Government spending moves IS, not LM.

    • Coincident — IIP, GDP.
    • Lagging — unemployment rate, interest rates.
  • Policy responses: in a recession, rate cuts and fiscal stimulus; in a boom, tightening.
  • Recovery shapes: V (sharp fall, sharp rebound), U, L (long stagnation), K (divergent sectors), W (double dip).
B6:
Syllabus: Tools of monetary policy · How monetary policy in India responded to the Global Financial Crisis · Fiscal policy & FRBM (see B8). This is the highest-frequency chapter in the PYQs (45 questions, asked in all 7 sessions).

1. In simple words

Monetary policy is how RBI controls the cost and quantity of money in the economy, so that prices stay stable while growth continues. RBI does this mainly by changing the rate at which banks borrow from it (the repo rate) and by adding or removing liquidity (cash) from banks.

Branch example: RBI cuts repo by 25 bps. Your bank's EBLR-linked home loans (repo + spread) reset lower at the next reset, which must be within 3 months. Deposit rates follow with a lag. More borrowing → more spending → growth. The reverse happens when RBI hikes.

2. The framework (RBI Act, amended 2016)

  • Objective (Preamble / Sec 45ZA): price stability while keeping growth in mind — Flexible Inflation Targeting (FIT), recommended by the Urjit Patel Committee (2014) and adopted in 2016.
  • Target: CPI-Combined inflation of 4% ± 2% (band 2–6%). It is set by the Central Government in consultation with RBI, every 5 years. new Retained for 1 Apr 2026 – 31 Mar 2031.
  • Failure = inflation outside the band for 3 consecutive quarters. RBI then reports to the Government with reasons, remedial action and a timeline (Sec 45ZN).
  • MPC (Sec 45ZB), formed in 2016, has 6 members:
    • 3 from RBI: the Governor (chair), the Deputy Governor in charge of monetary policy, and one RBI officer nominated by the Central Board.
    • 3 external members appointed by the Government, for 4 years with no re-appointment.
    It meets at least 4 times a year (in practice 6). Quorum is 4. Decisions are by majority; in a tie the Governor has a casting vote. Minutes are published on the 14th day. Members keep a silent period from 7 days before to 7 days after each meeting.

3. Tools of monetary policy

Quantitative (general)Qualitative (selective)
CRR, SLR, Bank Rate, repo / reverse repo / SDF (LAF), MSF, OMOs, MSS, LTRO/TLTRO, VRR/VRRR, forex swapsMargin requirements on loans against goods/shares, selective credit control, credit rationing, moral suasion, direct action
ToolMeaningKey facts
RepoRBI lends to banks against G-secs (sell now, buy back later)Policy rate. Injects liquidity. 5.25% (June 2026)
SDF (Apr 2022)Banks park surplus with RBI without collateralFloor of the corridor, 5.00%. The SDF balance counts for SLR. Replaced the fixed reverse repo as the floor
Reverse repoRBI borrows from banks giving G-secs as collateralAbsorbs liquidity. Kept at 3.35%, no longer the floor
MSF (May 2011)Overnight borrowing by SCBs when the market is tightCeiling, 5.50%. Banks may dip into SLR up to 2% of NDTL. A "safety valve"
Bank RateRediscount / long-term lending rate (the "discount rate")Aligned to MSF (5.50%). Penal rates are linked to it
CRR% of NDTL kept as cash with RBIRBI Act Sec 42. 3% (cut from 4% in 4 tranches, Sep–Nov 2025). No interest, no floor or ceiling. Fortnightly average, with at least 90% on every day
SLR% of NDTL kept by the bank in cash, gold, unencumbered approved securitiesBR Act Sec 24. 18%. Ceiling 40%, no floor
OMORBI buys or sells G-secs in the secondary marketPurchase → injects money, yields ↓. Sale → absorbs, yields ↑. Outright or repo-type
MSS (2004)Special T-bills/dated securities issued to sterilise surplus liquidity, e.g., from forex inflowsProceeds are kept in a separate account, not spent by the Government
LTRO / TLTRO (2020)Long-term repos at the repo rateTenors 1 & 3 years. TLTRO funds went to corporate bonds/CP/NCDs; TLTRO 2.0 required 50% in small/mid NBFCs & MFIs

Corridor picture: SDF 5.00 ← Repo 5.25 → MSF / Bank Rate 5.50 (each ±25 bps). Stance: neutral (June 2026). FY27 projections: GDP 6.6%, CPI 5.1%.

4. Lending-rate benchmarks (transmission)

  • BPLR (2003) → Base Rate (2010) → MCLR (1 Apr 2016) → EBLR (1 Oct 2019).
  • MCLR = marginal cost of funds + negative carry on CRR + operating costs + tenor premium. It is published for overnight, 1M, 3M, 6M and 1Y (no 2-month MCLR). Lending rate = MCLR + spread.
  • EBLR is mandatory for new floating-rate retail and MSE loans. Benchmark options: RBI repo, FBIL 3-month T-bill, FBIL 6-month T-bill, or another FBIL benchmark. The rate must reset at least once in 3 months.
  • MCLR and BPLR are bank-level rates, not RBI policy rates.

5. How monetary policy responded to the Global Financial Crisis (2008-09)

  • Repo cut from 9% to 4.75% (Oct 2008 – Apr 2009); reverse repo from 6% to 3.25%.
  • CRR cut from 9% to 5%; SLR from 25% to 24%.
  • Special liquidity windows: special repo for banks to fund MFs and NBFCs, refinance to SIDBI, NHB and EXIM, a forex swap window for banks' overseas branches, and relaxed ECB/FCNR rules.
  • Lesson: conventional rate cuts plus targeted liquidity. The same approach was reused in COVID-19 (LTRO, TLTRO, moratorium).
Traps:
  • CRR is RBI Act 42 and SLR is BR Act 24 — examiners swap them.
  • The MSF rate is ABOVE repo.
  • RBI pays NO interest on CRR.
  • The target is set by the Government, not RBI.
  • SDF needs no collateral, but the reverse repo does.
  • Hawkish = tightening.
  • Repo injects liquidity; reverse repo and SDF absorb it.

Check yourself

Under what situation does RBI have to report failure?Average CPI inflation above 6% or below 2% for 3 consecutive quarters (Sec 45ZN).
A bank has NDTL ₹5,000 cr. CRR?3% × 5,000 = ₹150 crore, kept with RBI and earning no interest.

Syllabus: National income & GDP concepts — computation, utility. 21 PYQs, asked in all 7 sessions; the most frequent home of calculation questions.

1. In simple words

GDP is the market value of all final goods and services produced within the country in a year. Everything else is an adjustment to it:

  • Gross → Net: subtract depreciation.
  • Domestic → National: add net factor income from abroad (NFIA).
  • Market price → Factor cost: subtract indirect taxes and add subsidies.

2. The formula ladder

AggregateFormula
GDP at market prices (GDPmp)C + I + G + (X − M)
GNPmpGDPmp + NFIA
NDPmpGDPmp − Depreciation (consumption of fixed capital)
NNPmpGNPmp − Depreciation = GDPmp + NFIA − Depreciation
… at factor cost… at MP − Indirect taxes + Subsidies
National IncomeNNP at factor cost
Per capita incomeNational income ÷ population
GVA at basic pricesValue of output − Intermediate consumption
GVA at factor costGVA(basic) − Production taxes + Production subsidies
GDPmpGVA(basic) + Product taxes − Product subsidies
GDP deflatorNominal GDP ÷ Real GDP × 100
  • Nominal GDP = current prices. Real GDP = constant (base-year) prices.
  • Personal income → minus direct taxes → personal disposable income.

3. Three methods of computation

MethodAdds up
Production / value-addedGVA of all sectors (output − intermediate consumption). Avoids double counting
IncomeCompensation of employees + operating surplus (rent, interest, profit) + mixed income of the self-employed (+ production taxes, depreciation to reach GDP)
ExpenditurePrivate final consumption + government final consumption + gross capital formation + net exports
  • In India the NSO (MoSPI) compiles GDP. Estimates come out in stages: advance estimates (Jan), provisional estimates (end-May), and quarterly estimates about 2 months after each quarter.
  • new Base year 2022-23 (series released 27 Feb 2026), replacing 2011-12. The new series uses GST, PFMS and e-Vahan data, double deflation and supply-use tables.
  • IIBF book / May 2023 key: GDP in India is "mainly calculated using the expenditure method". Know this keyed answer, though NSO's primary estimate is production-side.

4. Utility and limitations

  • Uses: measuring growth and the size of the economy, comparing countries and periods, per capita welfare, sector shares, guiding fiscal and monetary policy and planning, the base for ratios (deficit/GDP, debt/GDP, credit/GDP).
  • Limitations: ignores non-market work (household services), the informal sector is hard to capture, says nothing about distribution, ignores environmental damage and leisure, and has price-base problems.
Practise these:
  • GDPmp 1000, Dep 0.05, IT 5, Sub 3 → NDPfc = 1000 − 0.05 − 5 + 3 = 997.95.
  • GDPmp 22, NFIA 3, Dep 2.4 → NNPmp = 22.6.
  • Output 875, IC 460, prod. taxes 40, subsidies 15 → GVA(FC) = 390.
  • C 100, I 100, G 200, X 100, M 100 → GDP = 400.
Traps:
  • NFIA is used only for national aggregates, never for domestic ones.
  • Government consumption is an expenditure-method item, not an income item.
  • Transfer payments (pensions, subsidies, scholarships) are not part of GDP.
  • The base year is now 2022-23.

Why use value added instead of total sales?To avoid double counting intermediate goods.
B8:
Syllabus: Fiscal policy & FRBM Act · Union Budget — receipts, expenditure, plan expenditure, deficit concepts. 17 PYQs; calculations asked in Oct 2024 and Nov 2025.

1. Fiscal policy

  • Fiscal policy is the Government's use of taxation and public expenditure (and borrowing) to influence demand, growth, employment, prices and distribution. Keynes made it central to macro-stabilisation.
  • Counter-cyclical: in a slowdown spend more or tax less (expansionary); when overheating spend less or tax more (contractionary).
  • Monetary policy belongs to RBI; fiscal policy belongs to the Government.

2. The Union Budget

  • Constitutionally the Annual Financial Statement (Article 112). Presented on 1 February since 2017; the Railway Budget was merged into it the same year.
  • Government funds:
    • Consolidated Fund of India (Art 266) — all receipts and expenditure.
    • Contingency Fund (Art 267) — emergencies.
    • Public Account — e.g., provident funds and small savings, where the Government is only a banker.
  • The plan / non-plan classification of expenditure was abolished from 2017-18. Expenditure is now classified only as revenue vs capital.
ReceiptsExamples
Revenue — taxDirect: income tax, corporation tax. Indirect: GST (since July 2017; GST 2.0 slabs of 5% and 18% plus 40% demerit rate, from 22 Sept 2025), customs, excise
Revenue — non-taxInterest receipts, dividends & profits (RBI, PSUs), fees, fines, external grants
Capital — debtMarket borrowings (G-secs, T-bills), small savings / securities against them, external loans
Capital — non-debtRecoveries of loans & advances, disinvestment / miscellaneous capital receipts
ExpenditureExamples
RevenueCreates no asset or liability reduction: salaries, pensions, interest, subsidies, grants to states, running of departments
CapitalCreates assets or reduces liabilities: roads, defence capital outlay, loans to PSUs/states, repayment of debt

3. Deficit concepts

DeficitFormula
Revenue deficitRevenue expenditure − Revenue receipts
Effective revenue deficitRevenue deficit − Grants for creation of capital assets
Fiscal deficitTotal expenditure − (Revenue receipts + Non-debt capital receipts) = the total borrowing requirement
Primary deficitFiscal deficit − Interest payments (borrowing needed for current spending, excluding past debt)
Worked example (Nov 2025 PYQ):
  • Revenue receipts = 3.5 + 4.6 + 0.7 + 0.4 = 9.2.
  • Non-debt capital receipts = recoveries 0.3 + disinvestment 0.5 = 0.8.
  • Total expenditure = 4.2 + 2.4 + 1.1 + 1.5 + 2.7 + 0.4 = 12.3.
  • Fiscal deficit = 12.3 − 10.0 = 2.3. Primary deficit = 2.3 − interest 4.2 = −1.9 (a primary surplus).

4. FRBM Act 2003 and the N.K. Singh review

  • Objectives: long-term macro stability with revenue surpluses, prudent debt management, fiscal transparency, a medium-term fiscal framework, and removing fiscal impediments to monetary policy.
  • Targets: fiscal deficit at 3% of GDP; eliminate the revenue deficit. Three statements must be laid with the Budget: Medium-Term Fiscal Policy, Fiscal Policy Strategy, and Macro-economic Framework.
  • N.K. Singh Committee (2017):
    • Debt as the primary anchor: 60% of GDP for general government (Centre 40%, States 20%), originally by 2023.
    • An autonomous Fiscal Council (chair + 2 members).
    • Escape clause, and deviation only on the Council's advice.
    The 2018 amendment adopted debt targets with FD at 3%.
new Budget 2026-27:
  • Fiscal deficit 4.3% of GDP (FY26: 4.4%).
  • Central debt-to-GDP 55.6%, on a glide path to 50 ± 1% by 2030-31.
  • Total expenditure ₹53.5 lakh crore; capital expenditure ₹12.2 lakh crore; net tax receipts ₹28.7 lakh crore.
Traps:
  • Customs is a TAX revenue.
  • Disinvestment and loan recoveries are non-debt capital receipts; market borrowing is debt.
  • Fiscal deficit = borrowings.
  • Primary deficit removes interest.
  • Effective RD removes grants for capital assets.
  • Keynes, not Pigou, linked fiscal policy to output.

Check yourself

FD 12.5, interest 1.8 → primary deficit?10.7.
Is repayment of a loan by a state government to the Centre a debt receipt?No — it is a non-debt capital receipt (recovery of loans).
C1:
Syllabus: What is a financial system · Phase I pre-1951 · Phase II 1951 to mid-eighties · Phase III post-nineties · Narasimham Committee (1991) · Reform of the banking sector (1992–2008) · Present status. 17 PYQs.

1. What is a financial system?

The network that moves savings from those who have surplus money (households) to those who need it (businesses and government). It has four parts:

  • Institutions — banks, NBFCs, insurers, MFs, DFIs.
  • Markets — money, capital, forex, derivatives.
  • Instruments — deposits, shares, bonds, T-bills.
  • Services — payments, advisory, custody.

It also has regulators (RBI, SEBI, IRDAI, PFRDA, IBBI).

  • Formal system: organised, institutional and regulated — regulators, intermediaries, non-intermediaries (DFIs that lend directly to corporates) and other institutions.
  • Informal system: moneylenders, indigenous bankers, chit groups, friends and relatives. Low transaction cost, unstructured procedures, but high interest and no regulation.

2. Phases of development (as per syllabus)

PhaseMain features
I: Pre-1951Largely private, unregulated, urban-centred banking; many bank failures.
  • Presidency banks (Bengal 1806/1809, Bombay 1840, Madras 1843) merged into the Imperial Bank (1921).
  • Hilton Young Commission (1926) recommended a central bank → RBI (1 Apr 1935).
  • Banking Regulation Act 1949; RBI nationalised 1949.
II: 1951 – mid-1980sPlanning era; the state directs credit.
  • Institutions: SBI 1955 (from the Imperial Bank), LIC 1956, DICGC 1962, UTI 1964, IDBI 1964.
  • Nationalisation: 14 banks in 1969, 6 in 1980.
  • Priority sector lending, Lead Bank Scheme (1969), RRBs (1975), NABARD (1982), EXIM (1982).
  • Administered interest rates and high CRR/SLR ("financial repression").
III: Post-1990sLiberalisation.
  • Narasimham Committees; interest rates deregulated; CRR/SLR cut.
  • New private banks (1993); SEBI made statutory (1992); NSE (1992); IRDA (1999).
  • Technology, Basel norms, financial inclusion, payment banks and SFBs (2015-16), IBC (2016).

Some PYQs use a 4-phase version: I pre-independence · II post-independence · III post-liberalisation (1991–2007) · IV post-global financial crisis (2008 onwards). LIC (1956) falls in Phase II in both versions.

3. Narasimham Committee I (1991) — Committee on the Financial System

  • Reduce SLR (from 38.5% to 25% over 5 years) and CRR progressively.
  • Capital adequacy 8% (Basel I) in phases.
  • Prudential norms: income recognition, asset classification, provisioning (IRAC).
  • Deregulate interest rates; phase out directed credit (priority sector to be cut to 10% — not accepted).
  • Abolish branch licensing; free entry of private and foreign banks.
  • 4-tier banking structure:
    1. 3–4 large international banks.
    2. 8–10 national banks.
    3. Local banks.
    4. Rural banks.
  • Asset Reconstruction Fund for bad debts; special tribunals for recovery (→ DRTs, 1993).

4. Banking reforms 1992–2008

  • Prudential norms (IRAC 1992-93; 90-day NPA norm from 2004). CRAR 8% then 9%.
  • Interest deregulation (lending rates freed; BPLR 2003). New private banks: 1993 guidelines (UTI/Axis, ICICI, HDFC…).
  • DRTs (RDDBFI Act 1993); SARFAESI (2002); CIBIL (2000); Lok Adalats; Corporate Debt Restructuring (2001).
  • Technology: core banking, RTGS (2004), NEFT (2005). Basel II from 2008.
  • Narasimham II (1998) — Committee on Banking Sector Reforms: universal banking, mergers of strong banks, higher CRAR (10%), closing weak banks.

5. Present status (2026)

  • 12 PSBs after the 2019–20 mergers (BoB ← Dena + Vijaya; PNB ← OBC + United; Canara ← Syndicate; Union ← Andhra + Corporation; Indian ← Allahabad).
  • Also: private banks, foreign banks, SFBs, payment banks, RRBs (consolidated to 28 from 1 May 2025, "One State One RRB"), co-operative banks.
  • Strong balance sheets, low NPAs, digital public infrastructure (UPI, Account Aggregators).

  • Narasimham I said 8% CRAR (not 10%) and a 4-tier structure.
  • Universal banking was Narasimham II.
  • Moneylenders are informal.
  • Andhra, Vijaya and Corporation banks were nationalised in 1980, not 1969.

Syllabus: Functions · Development of banking · SCBs — types & functions · Local Area Banks · RRBs · Co-operative banks — types · Payment Banks & SFBs · NBFCs · Key RBI guidelines. 16 PYQs.

1. Functions of banks

  • Primary: accepting deposits and lending (BR Act Sec 5(b) defines banking as accepting deposits repayable on demand or otherwise, withdrawable by cheque, for lending or investment).
  • Secondary: agency services (collections, payments, standing instructions) and utility services (lockers, guarantees, LCs, remittances).
  • Para-banking (Sec 6): insurance, MF distribution, DP, cards, merchant banking.

2. Structure

  • Short-term rural (3-tier): State Co-operative Bank → District Central Co-operative Bank → PACS at village level.

  • Urban Co-operative Banks: mostly retail lending to individuals and MSMEs in non-rural areas. Limited non-fund and corporate exposure. Most cannot deal in forex directly. Four-tier regulatory framework (2022), PSL 60% (2025).
  • Dual control: registrar of co-operative societies (management) and RBI (banking). The BR (Amendment) Act 2020 strengthened RBI's powers. StCBs and DCCBs are supervised by NABARD.
  • Co-operative banks are the most numerous banks in India.

4. Key RBI guidelines and recent changes

  • Fit-and-proper criteria for directors; ownership caps in private banks (promoter up to 26% after 15 years).
  • new Banking Laws (Amendment) Act 2025: up to 4 nominees per deposit account/locker; "substantial interest" threshold raised from ₹5 lakh to ₹2 crore; longer tenure for co-operative bank directors.
  • Fintech (finance firm using technology, e.g., P2P lending) vs techfin (tech firm offering finance, e.g., WhatsApp Pay). Neo-banks are digital front-ends partnering with licensed banks.
  • NBFCs: see chapter C6.

  • WhatsApp Pay = techfin.
  • Scheduled-bank criteria are in the RBI Act (Sec 42(6)).

Syllabus (Reforms & developments): Bad banks · Infrastructure financing · Formation/role of NaBFID · Basic concepts of EASE.

1. Bad bank: NARCL + IDRCL

A "bad bank" takes large stressed loans off banks' books so that banks can focus on fresh lending.

  • NARCL (National Asset Reconstruction Co., Budget 2021): an ARC that buys large NPAs (₹500 crore+). It pays 15% in cash and 85% in Security Receipts, guaranteed by the Government of India. PSBs hold 51%.
  • IDRCL (India Debt Resolution Co.): the service/operating company that manages and resolves the assets, using market professionals. PSBs and PSFIs hold up to 49%; private lenders the rest.
  • Benefits: frees bank balance sheets and capital, aggregates exposures for faster resolution, and creates a market for stressed assets.
  • Other ARCs are regulated by RBI under SARFAESI (minimum NOF ₹300 crore). ARCIL was the first ARC (2002).

2. Infrastructure financing

  • Features: huge investment, long gestation, economies of scale, externalities. Banks face an asset-liability mismatch (short-term deposits vs long-term loans).
  • Channels: Government budgets, DFIs (NaBFID, IIFCL 2006), banks, NBFC-IFCs, insurance and pension funds, bonds, InvITs, Infrastructure Debt Funds.
  • National Infrastructure Pipeline (₹111 lakh crore); National Monetisation Pipeline.

3. NaBFID (NaBFID Act 2021)

  • A statutory DFI for infrastructure with both financial and developmental objectives:
    • Lending, refinancing and guarantees for infrastructure located wholly or partly in India.
    • Developing the bond, loan and derivatives markets.
  • Authorised capital ₹1 lakh crore (shares of ₹10). The Government initially held 100%, and must always hold at least 26%.
  • Others who may hold shares: multilateral institutions, sovereign wealth funds, pension/insurance funds, banks.
  • Raises money through bonds and loans; does not accept public deposits. Finances private projects as well as public ones.
  • Regulated by RBI as an AIFI. The board includes some independent directors.

4. EASE (Enhanced Access & Service Excellence)

  • A PSB reform agenda launched in 2018 (EASE 1.0) with IBA and BCG. Aim: institutionalise CLEAN and SMART banking.
  • The EASE Index scores each PSB on 120+ objective metrics.
  • Themes:
    • 1.0 — governance, prudential lending, customer responsiveness, credit off-take, financial inclusion, digital.
    • 2.0 and 3.0 — smart lending, tech-enabled banking.
    • 4.0 and later — customer-centric digital banking.
NaBFID has both financial and developmental goals (not "only developmental"). NARCL buys; IDRCL resolves. 15 : 85, not 20 : 80.

1. In simple words

The money market is where funds are borrowed and lent for up to one year. Banks use it to manage day-to-day cash: a branch network collects deposits unevenly, CRR must be met every day, and the treasury borrows or lends overnight to balance the books. It is regulated by RBI, under Chapter IIID of the RBI Act (Sec 45W).

Treasury example: on reporting Friday your bank is ₹500 crore short of CRR. The dealer borrows in the call market overnight, or borrows through TREPS against G-secs, or, as a last resort, uses MSF at 5.50%.

2. Call, notice and term money (all uncollateralised)

  • Rates are market-determined. Deals are on NDS-Call or reported within 15 minutes.

3. Treasury Bills

  • Short-term GoI debt issued by RBI through auctions, as zero-coupon discount instruments.
  • Tenors: 91, 182 and 364 days only. Distractors seen in PYQs: 271, 273, 274, 94.
  • Minimum ₹25,000 and multiples. Multiple-price auctions on e-Kuber. Non-competitive bids up to 5% of the notified amount.
  • Cash Management Bills (CMBs): under 91 days, to cover the Government's temporary cash mismatches.
  • T-bills are SLR-eligible.
T-bill yield = (Face value − Price) ÷ Price × 365 ÷ days × 100.
A 91-day bill at ₹98.50: 1.5 ÷ 98.5 × 365 ÷ 91 = 6.11%.

4. Certificate of Deposit (CD)

  • A negotiable, unsecured money-market deposit instrument, issued in demat form.
  • Issuers: SCBs (not RRBs) — including SFBs — and select All-India FIs. Co-operative banks and RRBs cannot issue CDs.
  • Minimum ₹5 lakh, in multiples of ₹5 lakh.
  • Tenor: banks 7 days to 1 year; FIs 1 to 3 years.
  • Issued at a discount, redeemed at par (face value).
  • Banks cannot lend against CDs. CRR and SLR apply to CDs (they are bank liabilities).
  • OTC trades must be reported within 15 minutes on F-TRAC (CCIL).

5. Commercial Paper (CP)

  • An unsecured promissory note issued at a discount.
  • Issuers: companies, NBFCs/HFCs, AIFIs.
  • Tenor 7 days to 1 year. Minimum ₹5 lakh and multiples.
  • Minimum credit rating A3. An issuer raising ₹1,000 crore or more in a year needs ratings from two CRAs.
  • IIBF book: tangible net worth at least ₹4 crore. A bank acts as the Issuing & Paying Agent (IPA).

6. Repo, market repo and tri-party repo

  • Repo: sell securities now with an agreement to repurchase later at a higher price — a collateralised loan. The seller is the borrower. Reverse repo is the same deal seen from the lender's side.
  • Market repo in G-secs, T-bills, SDLs and corporate bonds, among banks, PDs, MFs, insurers, NBFCs and others. A haircut is applied to the collateral.
  • Tri-party repo: a third-party agent handles collateral selection, payment & settlement, and custody & management.
    • Agent eligibility: at least ₹25 crore paid-up capital.
    • CCIL's TREPS (Tri-party Repo Dealing & Settlement, Nov 2018) replaced CBLO.

7. Bill Rediscounting Scheme (BRDS) and LTRO

  • BRDS: a bank that has discounted genuine trade bills rediscounts them with another bank or FI to raise short-term funds. The bill is discounted twice ("double discounting"). Only genuine trade bills are eligible, not accommodation bills.
  • LTRO (Feb 2020) and TLTRO (Mar 2020): RBI repos of 1-year and 3-year tenor at the repo rate, to improve transmission and credit. TLTRO funds went to corporate bonds, CP and NCDs (TLTRO 2.0: 50% to small/mid NBFCs and MFIs).
Traps:
  • The money market is up to 1 year; an SDL is NOT a money-market instrument.
  • Notice money runs up to 14 days, not 7.
  • CDs: co-op banks and RRBs cannot issue; SFBs can.
  • CP minimum rating is A3, not A2.
  • Both CDs and CPs are issued at a discount and redeemed at par.
  • NBFCs are not call-market participants.

4. RBI Retail Direct Scheme (Nov 2021)

  • Individual retail investors, including NRIs eligible under FEMA, open a free Retail Direct Gilt (RDG) account with RBI. Companies are not eligible.
  • Primary auctions: non-competitive bids. Secondary trades: NDS-OM odd-lot/RFQ segments.
  • Instruments: GoI dated securities, T-bills, SDLs, SGBs. No corporate bonds.
  • Requirements: rupee SB account, PAN, KYC, e-mail and mobile number.

5. Bond valuation and theorems

Bond price = present value of all coupons + present value of the face value, discounted at the market yield (YTM).

  • If coupon = yield → price = par. If yield > coupon → discount. If yield < coupon → premium.
  • Current yield = annual coupon ÷ market price. YTM = the IRR of holding the bond to maturity.
Malkiel's bond theorems:
  1. Price moves inversely to yield.
  2. Longer maturity → larger price change for a given yield change.
  3. That sensitivity rises with maturity, but at a decreasing rate.
  4. The price rise for a yield fall is greater than the price fall for an equal yield rise (convexity).
  5. Lower coupon → higher price sensitivity.
Worked example: a ₹100 bond, 8% coupon, 1 year left, market yield 10% → price ≈ 108 ÷ 1.10 = ₹98.18 (discount). Current yield at that price = 8 ÷ 98.18 = 8.15%.

6. Corporate bonds and ICDs

  • Corporate bonds / debentures are regulated by SEBI.
    • Credit rating is mandatory for public issues; a debenture trustee is required (for maturity over 18 months, per the book).
    • Private placements go through the Electronic Book Provider (EBP) platform.
    • Repo in corporate bonds is allowed. Companies raise long-term funds this way.
  • Inter-Corporate Deposits (ICDs) are unsecured short-term loans or deposits between companies, governed by Companies Act Sec 186 limits. Banks cannot finance NBFCs for making ICDs.
Traps:
  • PDs are registered with RBI.
  • Longer maturity means MORE sensitivity, and so does a lower coupon.
  • Retail Direct: no companies, no corporate bonds.
  • Name format is "7.25% GOI 2033", not "GOI 7.25%".
  • SDL coupon is half-yearly.
  • Settlement T+1 means the next WORKING day (a Friday deal settles Monday).
